records.claim: The Carrington Event was the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history, peaking on 1–2 September 1859 during solar cycle 10.
records.passage: The Carrington Event was the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history, peaking on 1–2 September 1859 during solar cycle 10.

records.claim: It created strong auroral displays that were reported globally and caused sparking and even fires in telegraph stations.
records.passage: It created strong auroral displays that were reported globally and caused sparking and even fires in telegraph stations.

records.claim: Telegraph systems all over Europe and North America failed, in some cases giving their operators electric shocks.
records.passage: Because of the geomagnetically induced current from the electromagnetic field, telegraph systems all over Europe and North America failed, in some cases giving their operators electric shocks.

records.claim: On 23 July 2012, a Carrington-class solar superstorm was observed, but its trajectory narrowly missed Earth by a margin of roughly nine days.
records.passage: On 23 July 2012, a "Carrington-class" solar superstorm (solar flare, CME, solar electromagnetic pulse) was observed, but its trajectory narrowly missed Earth by a margin of roughly nine days.

records.claim: In June 2013, researchers at Lloyd's of London and AER estimated the cost of a similar event in the present to the US alone at US$600 billion to $2.6 trillion.
records.passage: In June 2013, a joint venture from researchers at Lloyd's of London and Atmospheric and Environmental Research (AER) in the US used data from the Carrington Event to estimate the cost of a similar event in the present to the US alone at US$600 billion to $2.6 trillion (equivalent to $817 billion to $3.54 trillion in 2025), which, at the time, equated to roughly 3.6 to 15.5 percent of annual GDP.

narration.text: Why a repeat of 1859 could cost $2.6 trillion.
The 1859 Carrington storm set telegraph stations on fire.
Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed.
Some operators even got electric shocks.
In 2012, a similar storm missed Earth by about 9 days.
A 2013 estimate put a repeat's U.S. cost at $600 billion to $2.6 trillion.
Today, long power lines and satellites would take the hit.
So the same storm would cost far more now than then.
